title: Honor, simply
hookLine: Epictetus on reverence: think rightly of the gods and keep offerings honest and plain (Enchiridion 31)
last: KATHĒKON — WATCH WHAT YOU MUST DO.

lines: A CUP POURED ON THE GROUND.
THE FIRST BARLEY AT THE SHRINE.
cards: A small clay cup of wine, poured out on the ground before a meal. A handful of the first barley of the harvest, set at a household shrine.
In Epictetus' world, offerings like these belonged to ordinary household life, the way some families today light a candle, say grace, or leave flowers at a grave.
Section thirty-one of the handbook is about reverence, and what's striking is how little it asks for. Two things. Think rightly.

teach.h: FIRST: THINK RIGHTLY OF THE GODS.
teach.b: First, the thinking. The most important part of piety, Epictetus says, is to hold right opinions about the gods: that they exist, and that they govern the whole well and justly. That's his belief, a Stoic's.
People on their own path hold many different views here, and this lesson is about the shape of his advice more than his creed.
Why the thinking matters: hold that view, he says, and you can follow what happens willingly, and never blame the gods.
But only if you put good and bad in what's up to you. Put them in outside things, and every time you miss what you wanted, you'll feel cheated and resent whoever you think is in charge.
His hard example comes from the old stories: Eteocles and Polynices, brothers who killed each other over the throne of Thebes, because each thought the crown was the good.

teach.h: NOT CARELESS, STINGY, OR TOO MUCH.
teach.b: Farmers, sailors and merchants complain at the sky for the same reason. Then the giving. Pour the libations, make the offerings, give the first fruits, he says, according to the custom of your ancestors.
And do it purely. Not carelessly, not sloppily, not stingily, and not beyond what you can afford. You may not share his gods, or any gods.

teach.h: HONEST AND PLAIN, WHATEVER YOU HOLD.
teach.b: Still, a person can hold something sacred: a faith, the memory of a grandmother, a mountain, a quiet morning. His advice still fits. Don't make it a show, and don't let it go shabby.
Honor it honestly, within your means, in the way you were given. Simple isn't the same as small.

how: Epictetus advised keeping the customary offerings of one's ancestors, plainly and within one's means; some people on their own path today keep a small, simple ritual for whatever they hold sacred.

o: reverence shown by right thinking and plain giving
a lavish show of offerings that proves devotion
a public title given for brave deeds in war

p: by the custom of your ancestors

s: Epictetus says the biggest offering shows the most reverence
he says not beyond your means: purely, not carelessly, not stingily.
in Enchiridion 31, resentment of the gods comes from putting good in outside things
miss what you wanted, and you blame whoever you think is in charge.

games.q: the harvest is in, and your family's custom is to offer the first fruits. how does Epictetus say to give them?
o: as lavishly as possible, so everyone sees.
purely, not carelessly or stingily, and not beyond your means.
skip it. the gods don't need barley.
games.why: he keeps the custom of the ancestors, and asks only that it be done honestly and plainly, within what you can afford.

practice: Ask yourself what you hold sacred: God, a tradition, a person who's gone, the sea, or something you have no name for.

Picture one plain way to honor it, a candle lit, a minute of silence, a photo dusted, a walk to the water, or, if you pray, a prayer you already know. Choose one, and see yourself doing it carefully and without fuss.

wordCard.voice: Honor. In Enchiridion thirty-one, reverence comes in two parts: right thinking, and offerings made honestly, plainly, and within your means. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: reverence or piety, the subject of Enchiridion 31.

carryVoice: Your line: honestly, simply. No bigger than it needs to be, and no smaller. Day three hundred sixty-three, complete.

sources.ref: Eteocles and Polynices (e.g. Aeschylus, Seven Against Thebes)
